processing: Plantation tea from the highlands near Đà Lạt: green and black tea are the main products, with a smaller area of oolong; the early output was black tea.
harvest_season: Plantation picking across the growing season; no single prized picking is recorded.
appearance_dry: Twisted green leaf in the green tea lots, darker and more broken in the black.
appearance_wet: Mid-green leaf, typically machine-processed and fairly uniform.
taste_profile: As with other highland plantation greens, a clean, vegetal cup with moderate briskness; detailed tasting records for this estate are scarce.

brewing.notes: A plantation green that suits an everyday Western-style mug. Its black and oolong lots need hotter water.

vintage_note: Sold as current production by the Cầu Đất-Đà Lạt company and local shops, usually by product line and not by harvest year. The estate is also a tourist site, so much of it leaves as souvenir packs. As with other greens, drink within about a year.
description:
Cầu Đất is a highland tea area just outside Đà Lạt, in Lâm Đồng province, and one of the oldest plantations of its kind in the country. What makes it distinct is the colonial estate history more than one defined flavour.

The modern estate grows mainly green and black tea, with a small oolong area. The output is plantation-style, and the old factory, with machinery reportedly brought from Europe, now serves as a tea museum.

For the cup, expect what is typical of highland plantation green: clean and vegetal, with some briskness and few surprises. Do not treat it as a connoisseur tea unless a specific lot earns it.

The name is now also a tourist destination, the hills being a popular photo stop, so not everything sold nearby with the name necessarily comes from the estate. Buy from the company itself if origin matters to you.
history:
French operators established a tea estate here in 1927, known in Vietnamese as Sở trà Cầu Đất. At its height it is said to have covered over 600 hectares, producing mostly black tea for France and elsewhere in Europe. Earlier dates, including tea planted from 1922 and a survey of the area by Alexandre Yersin in 1893, appear in travel writing but are not firmly established.

As French activity wound down it passed to Chinese merchants around 1960, accounts differing on exact timing, and came under Lâm Đồng provincial management around 1975. It became the Cầu Đất-Đà Lạt Tea Joint Stock Company in 2005. Reported area today is about 220 to 230 hectares.
